opus-5.5.text:
I think people often underestimate them, and in a particular way.

When we talk about a "native" embodied foundation model, we mean one trained from the ground up around action and interaction with the physical world. That is different from taking a large vision-language model and attaching an action head. That difference changes the whole resource picture.

**Data comes first, and it's the hardest part.** Language models had the internet: trillions of tokens that already existed and just needed collecting. Embodied intelligence has nothing like that. Robot interaction data has to be produced deliberately, through teleoperation, real deployments, or simulation. Each trajectory costs hardware time, human operator time, and maintenance. So the bottleneck isn't only money. It's throughput: how many robots you can run in parallel, across how many diverse environments, and for how long. Diversity matters more than raw volume. A million demonstrations in one kitchen are worth far less than a hundred thousand across a thousand different scenes.

**Compute is significant but not the dominant constraint yet.** Native embodied models will need serious training compute, especially if we want them to absorb video and world-modeling objectives alongside action. But today I'd say most teams are data-limited before they are compute-limited. The compute curve will matter more once the data pipelines mature.

**Infrastructure is the hidden cost.** You need the whole loop: data collection platforms, cleaning and annotation, simulation that is realistic enough to be useful, and, most importantly, evaluation. Evaluating a language model is cheap. Evaluating a robot policy means running it in the real world, repeatedly, and that is slow and expensive. Without good evaluation, you can't tell whether your scaling is actually working.

**Talent is the last piece.** You need people who understand large-scale model training and people who understand hardware, control, and real-world deployment, and they need to work as one team. That combination is still rare.

So my view is that this is not a game you win just by raising the most money and buying the most GPUs. It's closer to building an industrial system. The teams that make progress will be the ones that build an efficient data flywheel, where deployment produces data, data improves the model, and a better model enables wider deployment. Resources matter enormously, but how efficiently you turn them into useful interaction data matters even more.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes training a native model from attaching an action head to a vision-language model and describes costly data and infrastructure needs. It does not clearly state that native-model pretraining requires far more resources than treating embodied AI as a downstream application of digital-world models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most underestimated questions in the field right now. People look at embodied AI and assume it's just "LLM plus a robot," so the resource curve must look like the language model curve. It doesn't, and in some ways it's harder.

The first thing is data. With language models, the internet already did the data collection for you. Humanity spent twenty years writing text onto servers, and you just scrape it. For a native embodied model, there is no equivalent. There's no internet of robot actions. You have to generate the data yourself, and that means real robots, real teleoperation, real physical environments, real time. One robot collecting one trajectory is minutes of effort for seconds of data. So the bottleneck isn't GPUs in the first instance, it's the pipeline that produces useful interaction data at scale. If you want to push this seriously, you end up building a data factory before you build a model.

The second thing is that compute shifts shape. Training a large vision-language-action model is still expensive, but the more interesting cost is simulation and iteration. You need a lot of rollouts, a lot of sim-to-real cycles, a lot of evaluation that can't be done purely offline. A language model you can evaluate on a benchmark in an afternoon. An embodied model you have to actually run in the world, and the world doesn't parallelize nearly as nicely as a cluster does.

Third, hardware itself. If your model is truly native, meaning designed around the embodiment rather than retrofitted onto it, then the model and the body co-evolve. That means you're not just buying robots, you're iterating on robots. Sensors, actuators, latency budgets. Every time the body changes, some fraction of the data and the model has to be revisited. That's a hidden tax that software-only labs never pay.

So my overall view is that the resource requirement is less about raw scale and more about breadth. You need capital, yes, but you also need a team that spans hardware, data operations, simulation and model training, all sitting close enough to each other to iterate weekly. That's rare. I think that's why we'll see fewer serious players here than in language, and why the ones who succeed will look more like a vertically integrated company than a traditional AI research lab.

The optimistic side is that the frontier isn't gated purely by who has the largest cluster. Clever data strategies, better simulation, leveraging video and human demonstration data, these can shift the curve a lot. So smaller teams aren't hopeless. But anyone who thinks they can do this with a model team alone is going to learn an expensive lesson.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied AI is harder and more resource-intensive than language-model development, but it does not state that pretraining native embodied models requires far more resources than treating embodied AI as a downstream application of digital-world models.

astra-6.text:
I think the resource requirements go well beyond compute. If we want a native embodied foundation model—one that learns perception and action together—we need a way to collect data from interactions with the physical world. That means hardware, environments, people operating and maintaining the systems, and a process for turning those interactions into useful training data.

The difficult part is getting enough diversity. Repeating one task on one robot can produce a lot of data, but that doesn’t necessarily teach the model to handle a new object or recover when something goes wrong. Simulation can help expand that coverage, but we still need real-world experience to understand where the model’s capabilities transfer.

So I’d think about this as an entire development loop: collecting data, training, deploying, seeing where the model fails, and collecting the next round of data. Compute is a major investment, but the efficiency of that loop may matter just as much. Before attaching a budget to it, I’d want to be very clear about how broad a range of tasks and environments we expect the model to handle.

r001.rationale: The response describes substantial resources for native embodied models, but it does not compare those requirements with treating embodied AI as a downstream application of digital-world models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the resource requirements are substantial, but it’s not simply a matter of buying more GPUs. For a native embodied foundation model, you need a complete loop: collecting data through interaction, training the model, deploying it on hardware, and using the failures to guide the next round of data collection.

Compute is one part of that. Another major part is the robots themselves, the environments they operate in, and the people who keep those systems running. Physical interaction is slower and more expensive than collecting text or images, and the data needs to cover different tasks, objects, and situations.

So I would look at resources in terms of the whole system. Simulation and existing visual data can help, but you still need real-world interaction to establish what transfers. The key question is how efficiently you can turn each interaction into an improvement in the model. That efficiency will matter as much as the absolute scale of the investment.

r001.rationale: The response describes substantial resources for native embodied models, including robots, environments, staff, and real-world interaction, but it does not compare those requirements with treating embodied AI as a downstream application of digital-world models.
